book.title: High-quality listening behaviors linked to social connection between strangers
book.author_credibility: Barbara Fredrickson (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill) is a highly cited emotion and positive-relationships researcher; the team has no overlap with the Kluger and Itzchakov listening group, so it provides independent evidence. Published open access in a Nature Portfolio journal.
book.evidence_base: Two preregistered studies (total N = 646). Study 1: 10-minute semi-structured deep-talk conversations with a trained confederate after a randomized social-connection versus breathing-control intervention; listening behaviors coded by observers. Study 2: brief small talk with an experimenter. Connection measured by observers, partners, self-report and conversational response times. Behavior-outcome links are correlational.

legal_access.note: Full open-access text via Europe PMC (PMC web page returned a captcha).

supports_existing.note: Independent, non-Gino evidence: in deep-talk conversations between strangers, observer-coded follow-up questions and verbal validation predicted connection rated by observers and partners, and a brief connection prompt increased follow-up questions, which in turn predicted connection.

Visible listening matters, but the authors note that verbal signals such as validation and follow-ups are stronger evidence of listening than nods or 'mhmm', which can be faked; in brief small talk, overall listening quality mattered more than counts of specific verbal moves.

Explicit verbal evidence of understanding (validation, follow-ups) linked to stronger connection and faster, smoother turn-taking, consistent with proving you are listening rather than just listening.

still_unverified: Not yet independently replicated; partners were a trained confederate (Study 1) and an experimenter (Study 2), which the authors flag as a limitation.

research_notes: Read the full text from Europe PMC. No new insight added: the findings strengthen existing follow-up-question and visible-listening insights rather than adding a distinct technique. The intervention did not increase listening in the small-talk study, and verbal validation did not increase with the intervention in Study 1.
